title: Ever-Tite Roofing Corp. v. Green
lead: Homeowners sign a roofing proposal allowing acceptance by commencing performance. While financing is processed, they hire another roofer without notice, and the original contractor’s dispatched crew arrives to find the job underway.

actors.name: G. T. Green and Jessie Fay Green
Ever-Tite Roofing Corporation
actors.role: Contractor seeking damages after mobilizing for the job.

actors.name: Ever-Tite’s sales representative
actors.role: Signer who lacked authority to accept for the corporation.

proceedings: The trial court dismissed because it viewed withdrawal as preceding actual roofing performance.
The Louisiana Court of Appeal reversed and rendered a $311.37 judgment with interest and costs, denying attorney’s fees.
limits: This transforms the canonical historical brief without a fresh audit or present Louisiana-law certification. Dispatch is described as June 18 or 19 in the source. The retrieved text lacks internal reporter markers, so pinpoints identify opinion discussions. Rehearing denial on November 29 does not replace the November 2 principal date.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Greens propose roofing on terms permitting two forms of acceptance
sections.cue: Why did the salesperson’s signature not complete the bargain?
paragraphs: G. T. Green and Jessie Fay Green wanted their Webster Parish residence re-roofed. On June 10, 1953, they signed an instrument specifying work and an installment price. Ever-Tite Roofing’s sales representative also signed but lacked corporate acceptance authority.

The form became binding upon written acceptance by a principal or authorized officer, or commencement of performance. It also contained no-cancellation, collection, and integration language. No authorized written acceptance followed, so any formation depended on the permitted performance route.

The homeowners knew their credit would be checked and financing obtained. The proposal reached Ever-Tite the next day. The company requested a credit report, transmitted it to the lender, and supplied requested additional information. The lender then approved financing.

sources.pinpoint: 83 So. 2d 449, quoted agreement and opening financing discussion

sections.title: The contractor mobilizes before receiving any withdrawal
sections.cue: What happened when its workers reached the house?
paragraphs: Immediately after approval, in the sequence described as June 18 or 19, Ever-Tite arranged workers and two trucks, loaded roofing materials in Shreveport, and transported crew and materials to the Greens’ home.

Another crew was already roofing it. The Greens said they had hired those workers two days earlier and would not allow Ever-Tite to proceed. They had sent no cancellation notice and had made no attempt to do so. Their later assertion that they did not know how to contact Ever-Tite conflicted with the conspicuous company name, address, and telephone number on their copy of the form.

sections.title: The trial court treats commencement as work on the roof
paragraphs: Ever-Tite sued for breach damages. The Greens contended that their proposal had not been accepted as specified before they withdrew. The trial court agreed, treating the refusal at arrival as preceding the start of actual roofing, and dismissed at Ever-Tite’s cost.

On appeal, Judge Ayres examined both whether the proposal remained open through financing and whether loading and dispatch counted as the commencement the form invited. The no-cancellation phrase did not replace that formation inquiry or by itself establish an immediately binding contract from the homeowners’ signatures.

sources.pinpoint: 83 So. 2d 449, opening procedure and formal-acceptance discussions

sections.title: The appellate court finds timely acceptance through mobilization
sections.cue: Why did an undisclosed competing contract not end the offer?
paragraphs: The form fixed no deadline. The work’s nature and known financing requirement allowed a reasonable interval, and Ever-Tite had diligently obtained and supplied credit information. The lender’s additional inquiry explained the delay. The court found neither unreasonable delay nor abandonment.

It discussed a Restatement lapse rule and Louisiana Civil Code provisions then in force. Article 1809 recognized revocation before acceptance while requiring the reasonable time contemplated by terms and circumstances. The holding therefore did not depend on an unqualified nationwide rule of instantaneous revocability.

In this roofing transaction, loading necessary materials and dispatching them with workers commenced performance. The trial court erred by limiting commencement to physical work on the house. The proposal expressly authorized acceptance through commencement, and these job-directed acts fulfilled it before communicated refusal.

Privately hiring someone else did not notify Ever-Tite. Given the displayed contact information, the Greens’ asserted inability to give notice was unpersuasive. Once they refused the already accepted performance, they breached.

sources.pinpoint: 83 So. 2d 449, diligence, Civil Code arts.1800–1809, acceptance, and notice discussions

sections.title: Uncontroverted expense and profit evidence permits a rendered judgment
paragraphs: Civil Code articles 1930 and 1934 supplied compensation for loss sustained and profit foregone. Ever-Tite proved $85.37 for loading, transportation, return unloading, and wasted-trip wages. Its manager established expected profit of $226. Neither component was contradicted.

The resulting $311.37 combined wasted mobilization and lost profit rather than the full price plus avoided costs, and included no punitive sum. Because the proof was complete, no damages remand was needed.

The form authorized attorney’s fees when placed with counsel for collection or collected through court. That language concerned collecting under the agreement, not damages for being prevented from performing. With no applicable contractual or legal authorization, the court refused fees.

On November 2, 1955, the Second Circuit Court of Appeal set aside dismissal and rendered judgment against both Greens for $311.37, with five-percent annual interest from judicial demand until payment and all costs. No separate opinion appeared; rehearing was denied November 29. The decision did not make every preparatory purchase an acceptance, but enforced this express commencement clause in its factual setting.

sources.pinpoint: 83 So. 2d 449, concluding damages, fees, and judgment discussions
